questions.q: Which level of Active Directory structure is the real administrative and security boundary, with its own domain controllers and database?
options: The Organizational Unit
The forest
The tree
The domain
questions.explain: A domain has its own domain controllers, its own copy of the AD database, and its own security policies. Trees and forests are broader namespace/trust groupings above it.

questions.q: What is a forest in Active Directory?
options: The outer AD boundary — one or more trees connected by trust relationships, sharing a schema and Global Catalog
A type of Group Policy Object
A container inside a domain used to organize users and computers
A single domain controller's local database
questions.explain: A forest is the outermost boundary in AD, made up of one or more trees that share a common schema and Global Catalog.

options: To replace the need for a domain controller
To act as a security boundary like a domain
To store the AD schema
To apply Group Policy Objects to a subset of objects and to delegate limited administrative control
questions.explain: OUs are administrative/organizational containers, not security boundaries — their whole purpose is scoping GPOs and delegated admin rights to a subset of objects.

questions.q: What does "delegation" mean in an Active Directory context?
options: Granting a specific person or group limited admin rights over one OU, without domain-wide access
Linking two separate forests together with a trust
Automatically replicating changes between domain controllers
Promoting a server to a domain controller
questions.explain: Delegation lets you grant scoped rights, such as password-reset permission over one OU's users, without giving domain-wide administrative access.

questions.q: In a realistic OU design, why are users and computers often split into separate sub-OUs within each department?
options: Because user-targeted GPOs (like mapped drives) and computer-targeted GPOs (like screen-lock timeouts) need to apply to the right kind of object only
Because Active Directory does not allow users and computers in the same OU
Because it reduces the number of domain controllers needed
Because it is required by the AD schema
questions.explain: Splitting users and computers into sub-OUs lets each kind of GPO target exactly the objects it should, since some policies apply to users and others apply to computers.
